pumac-2014-number-theory-b-01.title: Evaluate f(1)
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-01.body:
Let the roots be $r_1,r_2,r_3$ (distinct negative integers), so $f(x)=(x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3)$. Then
$$f(1)=1+a+b+c=2015=(1-r_1)(1-r_2)(1-r_3).$$
The numbers $1-r_i$ are distinct integers $\ge2$ and $2015=5\cdot13\cdot31$, so $\{1-r_i\}=\{5,13,31\}$ and the roots are $-4,-12,-30$. Then $c=f(0)=(-r_1)(-r_2)(-r_3)=4\cdot12\cdot30=1440$.

**Answer: 1440**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-02.title: Cycle of last digits
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-02.body:
The last digit of $17^k$ is the last digit of $7^k$, which cycles $7,9,3,1$ with period $4$, so it depends on $k\bmod4$. Here $k=17^{17^{17}}$ and $17\equiv1\pmod4$, so $k\equiv1\pmod4$. The last digit is that of $7^1$, namely $7$.

**Answer: 7**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-03.title: Bound the number of divisors by the number of prime factors
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-03.body:
If $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ then $\tau(n)=\prod(e_i+1)$. Since $2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310>1000$, a $3$-digit number has at most $4$ distinct prime factors.

- $1$ prime factor: $2^{10}>1000$, so at most $10$ divisors.
- $2$ prime factors: $2^6\cdot3^3>1000$, so (checking exponent pairs) at most $24$ divisors.
- $3$ prime factors: $2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5>1000$, so at most $30$ divisors.
- $4$ prime factors: $2^4\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7>1000$, so the best exponents are $(3,1,1,1)$ giving at most $4\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=32$ divisors, attained by $2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=840$.

So $840$ has the most divisors ($32$; a check of all $3$-digit numbers shows it is the only one with $32$).

**Answer: 840**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-04.title: Inclusion-exclusion on 2015
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-04.body:
The fractions are $\frac{k}{2015-k}$ for $k=1,\dots,1007$, and $\gcd(k,2015-k)=\gcd(k,2015)$ with $2015=5\cdot13\cdot31$. So we count $k\le1007$ not divisible by $5$, $13$ or $31$. Multiples among $1,\dots,1007$:
$$\lfloor\tfrac{1007}5\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{1007}{13}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{1007}{31}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{1007}{65}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{1007}{155}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{1007}{403}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{1007}{2015}\rfloor=201+77+32-15-6-2+0=287.$$
So $1007-287=720$ fractions are in lowest form.

**Answer: 720**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-05.title: Factor n squared minus 1
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-05.body:
$3\cdot2^x=(n-1)(n+1)$. The factors $n-1$ and $n+1$ differ by $2$, are positive (as $n\ge2$), and their product has no prime factor other than $2$ and $3$ (a single $3$). Two cases:

- $n+1=3\cdot2^a$, $n-1=2^b$: then $2^b=3\cdot2^a-2$. If $a=0$: $2^b=1$, $n=2$, $x=0$ (not positive). If $a=1$: $2^b=4$, $b=2$, $n=5$, $x=a+b=3$. If $a\ge2$: $3\cdot2^a-2\equiv2\pmod4$ and exceeds $2$, so it is not a power of $2$.
- $n+1=2^a$, $n-1=3\cdot2^b$: then $2^a=3\cdot2^b+2$. If $b=0$: $2^a=5$, impossible. If $b=1$: $2^a=8$, $a=3$, $n=7$, $x=a+b=4$. If $b\ge2$: $3\cdot2^b+2\equiv2\pmod4$ and exceeds $2$, so it is not a power of $2$.

So the positive solutions are $x=3$ ($n=5$: $3\cdot8=24=5^2-1$) and $x=4$ ($n=7$: $3\cdot16=48=7^2-1$). Their sum is $7$.

**Answer: 7**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-06.title: A mod 3 argument and an example
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-06.body:
Let $P=\prod A_i$. The equation $\sum1/A_i=1$ is equivalent to $P=\sum_iP/A_i$. Modulo $3$ every $A_i\equiv2$, so $P\equiv2^n$ and each $P/A_i\equiv2^{n-1}$; hence $2^n\equiv n\cdot2^{n-1}$, i.e. $n\equiv2\pmod3$. So $n\in\{2,5,8,\dots\}$.

- $n=2$: $\frac1A+\frac1B=1$ with $A,B\ge2$ forces $A=B=2$, not distinct.
- $n=5$: the five largest possible reciprocals are those of $2,5,8,11,14$, whose sum is $\frac12+\frac15+\frac18+\frac1{11}+\frac1{14}<1$ (about $0.987$), so no five distinct elements work.
- $n=8$ works:
$$\frac12+\frac15+\frac18+\frac1{11}+\frac1{14}+\frac1{80}+\frac1{6161}+\frac1{37951760}=1,$$
with $80\equiv6161\equiv37951760\equiv2\pmod3$. (Indeed $\frac12+\frac15+\frac18+\frac1{11}+\frac1{14}+\frac1{80}=1-\frac1{6160}$, and $\frac1{6160}=\frac1{6161}+\frac1{6161\cdot6160}$ with $6161\cdot6160=37951760$.)

So the minimum is $8$.

**Answer: 8**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-07.title: p preserves divisor sets
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-07.body:
Write $D(a)$ for the set of divisors of $a$ in $\{1,\dots,35\}$. If $d\mid a$ then $p(d)\mid p(a)$, so $p$ maps $D(a)$ injectively into $D(p(a))$, hence $\tau(p(a))\ge\tau(a)$ for every $a$. Since $p$ is a bijection, $\sum_a\tau(p(a))=\sum_a\tau(a)$, so equality holds termwise: $\tau(p(a))=\tau(a)$ and $p(D(a))=D(p(a))$.

- Primes go to primes. For a prime power $q^k\le35$, $D(q^k)$ is a chain of $k+1$ elements, so $p(q^k)=p(q)^k$ (a prime power with $k+1$ divisors).
- $p(32)=p(2)^5\le35$ forces $p(2)=2$. Then $p(27)=p(3)^3\le35$ gives $p(3)\in\{2,3\}$, so $p(3)=3$; and $p(25)=p(5)^2\le35$ gives $p(5)=5$.
- $p(7)$: $p(35)$ is divisible by $p(5)=5$ and $p(7)$ and has $4$ divisors, so $p(35)=5\,p(7)\le35$, i.e. $p(7)\le7$; the primes $2,3,5$ are taken, so $p(7)=7$. Similarly $p(33)=3\,p(11)\le35$ gives $p(11)\le11$, so $p(11)=11$.
- $13$ and $17$: $26=2\cdot13$ and $34=2\cdot17$ force $p(13),p(17)\le17$, so $\{p(13),p(17)\}=\{13,17\}$: $2$ choices.
- $19,23,29,31$ have no other multiples in the set, so they may be permuted arbitrarily: $4!=24$ choices.

A composite $a=\prod q_i^{k_i}$ must go to $\prod p(q_i)^{k_i}$ (it is a multiple of this product, which has the same number of divisors), and every such assignment is valid (e.g. $26\leftrightarrow34$ stays $\le35$). So there are $2\cdot24=48$ permutations.

**Answer: 48**

pumac-2014-number-theory-b-08.title: Solve for x
pumac-2014-number-theory-b-08.body:
Let $\frac{x+n}{x-n}=k^2$ with $k$ odd. Then $1+\frac{2n}{x-n}=k^2$, so $x-n=\frac{2n}{k^2-1}$ must be a nonzero integer ($k=1$ is impossible since it would give $n=0$). So $k\ge3$ and $(k^2-1)\mid2n$. For odd $k=2j+1$, $k^2-1=4j(j+1)$ is a multiple of $8$, so $8\mid2n$, i.e. $4\mid n$.

Conversely, if $4\mid n$ take $k=3$: $x=n+\frac n4=\frac{5n}4$, and $\frac{x+n}{x-n}=\frac{9n/4}{n/4}=9$.

So the valid $n$ are exactly the multiples of $4$ up to $2014$: $\lfloor2014/4\rfloor=503$.

**Answer: 503**
